title: Story Small-World & Retelling
strapline: A whole story you can hold in your hands — and tell again your own way.
intent: Children retell and reinvent familiar stories, internalising story language, structure and sequence.
Children hold a narrative in mind — beginning, middle, end — and use it to drive their play.
Children build rich spoken language, using the once-upon-a-time words and refrains of well-loved tales.
Children explore characters' feelings and motives, growing empathy and understanding of others.
Children move between a book and their own play, deepening comprehension and love of story.
implementation: Choose a story the children know deeply — The Three Billy Goats, We're Going on a Bear Hunt — and gather figures and props to match.
Set the scene with natural materials: a blue-fabric river, a pebble bridge, moss for the meadow, a cave of dark cloth.
Tell the story first with the props, using the repeated refrains, then step back and let children take over.
Follow the children's retelling without correcting — new endings and mash-ups are comprehension in action.
Feed in story language as you play alongside: 'suddenly...', 'once upon a time...', 'and they all lived...'.
Add a story map or sequencing cards nearby so children can order the events and mark-make their own version.
Rotate the story every week or two, keeping favourites available so retellings mature over time.
key_questions: What happens at the beginning of your story?
How is the troll feeling now — why?
What could happen next? Could you make a different ending?
Which part comes first, and which comes last?
Can you tell me the story in your own words?

impact.text: Children retell a familiar story in the right order using the props.
Children use story language and repeated refrains in their play.
Children invent new events and endings, showing they understand story.
Children talk about how characters feel and why they act.
Children sequence events — beginning, middle, end.
Children stay deeply engaged, extending the story over time.

enhancements: Story stones or story spoons painted with the characters.
A story map on the floor for the goats to cross or the bear-hunt journey.
A basket of the book plus small-world figures kept together.
Sequencing cards and a blank story strip for children to draw their retelling.
Puppets and a simple stage for a performed version.
A recording device so children can hear their own storytelling played back.

playing_exploring: Children step into the story world and make it their own.
They choose which story to tell and how the props are arranged.
active_learning: Children return to a favourite story again and again, deepening it each time.
They stay absorbed in a long, involved retelling.
creating_thinking: Children reshape stories, inventing new characters and endings.
They connect the book to their play, holding the whole narrative in mind.
